facts.title: Parameterised SQL keeps data out of the query's syntax
facts.fact: SQL injection occurs when an application concatenates or interpolates data into SQL text, so the database parses attacker-controlled characters as part of the statement. Parameterised queries keep the statement structure and the values on separate channels: the driver sends the template first and the values afterwards, so a value cannot alter the parse tree. Parameterisation protects values only. Table names, column names, sort directions and other identifiers still need a server-side allowlist because drivers cannot bind them.
details: Use the driver's placeholder style consistently: ? for sqlite3 and MySQL, %s for psycopg, :name for Oracle; pass a tuple or mapping, never an f-string.
For ORDER BY or dynamic columns, map the user's choice to a constant SQL fragment instead of concatenating it.
Stored procedures that build dynamic SQL internally must parameterise too; moving the string into the database does not remove the flaw.
pitfalls: Calling addslashes() or manual quote-doubling safe: multibyte encodings, numeric contexts and second-order storage defeat it.
Assuming an ORM removes injection: raw(), extra(), RawSQL and .raw() still pass text through.

code.issue: Concatenation lets a crafted email close the quote and append SQL; binding keeps the query structure fixed and treats the value as data. Identifiers such as column names still require an allowlist.

mcqs.question: Which change removes SQL injection in a value position?
options: Binding the value with a driver placeholder
Escaping single quotes in the value
Limiting the value to 64 characters
Returning a generic error message on failure
mcqs.rationale: Placeholders separate statement structure from data, so the value cannot be parsed as SQL. Escaping is fragile across charsets and numeric contexts, length limits do not remove metacharacters, and error handling affects disclosure only.

misconceptions.claim: Prepared statements exist mainly to speed up repeated queries.
misconceptions.correction: Caching is secondary. The security property is that the statement is parsed before the values arrive, so values are never syntax. Use parameterised queries even for one-shot statements.

facts.title: Reflected, stored and DOM XSS differ by delivery, not root cause
facts.fact: Reflected XSS places request data in the response that immediately follows the request; stored XSS persists the data and serves it to later visitors; DOM-based XSS is produced by client-side JavaScript that writes attacker-influenced data into a dangerous sink such as innerHTML. The three differ in delivery and persistence, not in the root cause: unencoded data reaching an HTML, attribute, URL, script or CSS context. Choosing the right defence starts with identifying the context the data enters, because HTML-entity encoding is wrong for a JavaScript string and useless inside a URL.
details: Reflected bugs commonly appear in search pages, error messages and redirect parameters; stored bugs in profiles, comments, tickets and file names.
DOM XSS may never reach the server, so server logs, WAF rules and server-side templating cannot see it.
Mutation XSS can appear after a sanitiser or the browser re-parses markup, so sanitise with a maintained library and test the final DOM.

mcqs.question: A page reads location.hash in JavaScript and assigns it to innerHTML. Which category is this?
options: DOM-based XSS
Stored XSS
Reflected XSS
CSRF
mcqs.rationale: The source is browser-side (location.hash) and the sink is browser-side (innerHTML), so the vulnerability lives in the DOM and may never involve a server response. Stored and reflected XSS require the payload to pass through the server.

references.title: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet
CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation

facts.title: Encode at the sink, for the exact context, not at the input
facts.fact: Output encoding converts data into a representation that is inert in the destination context, and it must happen at the sink where that context is known. HTML text needs entity encoding, attribute values need quoting plus entity encoding, JavaScript string literals need JavaScript escaping, URLs need percent-encoding, and CSS needs CSS escaping; one encoder cannot serve all five. Input validation reduces the range of data but cannot replace encoding, because the same valid string can be dangerous in a different context.
details: React escapes text children and most attribute values, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML bypasses escaping; use a maintained HTML sanitiser when rich text is a requirement.
URL-valued attributes need a scheme allowlist as well as encoding: encoding does not stop javascript: or data: schemes.
A strict Content-Security-Policy limits script execution after a bug but does not repair the output path; treat it as mitigation.
pitfalls: Sanitising on input and storing the result: the stored value is then trusted by every future context, including ones the sanitiser did not model.
Using a generic HTML encoder for JavaScript or URL contexts, where its output is not valid escaping.

code.issue: React escapes children, so text cannot become markup; dangerouslySetInnerHTML opts out and makes the caller responsible for sanitisation. Attribute contexts such as href still need scheme validation.

mcqs.question: Where should output encoding be applied?
options: Immediately before data is written into its destination context
Once, when data enters the application
Only when data is stored in the database
Only for data that failed input validation
mcqs.rationale: Encoding depends on the destination (HTML, attribute, JS, URL, CSS), which is known at the sink. Encoding on input loses that context and may be undone by later processing.

misconceptions.claim: Validating input against an allowlist removes the need for output encoding.
misconceptions.correction: Validation narrows the accepted values but does not know where they will be rendered. A perfectly valid name can still break out of an HTML attribute or a JavaScript string, so encoding at the sink remains necessary.

facts.title: Cookie attributes bound the damage of a stolen or forged cookie
facts.fact: Cookie attributes limit how a cookie travels and who can read it. Secure keeps it off plain HTTP, HttpOnly removes it from document.cookie and reduces the impact of XSS, SameSite controls cross-site sending, and the __Host- name prefix requires Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute so a sibling subdomain cannot overwrite it. For a session cookie, set Secure, HttpOnly and an explicit SameSite value rather than relying on browser defaults.
details: SameSite=None is only valid together with Secure and is needed for legitimate cross-site embedding.
Path is not an authorization boundary; scripts on the same origin can still read non-HttpOnly cookies belonging to other paths.
Max-Age and Expires control persistence; a session cookie that survives browser restart expands the theft window.

configs.snippet: Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=REDACTED; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=28800
configs.purpose: Issue a host-bound session cookie that is HTTPS-only, script-inaccessible and not sent on cross-site POSTs.

mcqs.question: Which attribute prevents JavaScript from reading a cookie?
options: HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite=Strict
Max-Age
mcqs.rationale: HttpOnly removes the cookie from document.cookie, so script injection cannot exfiltrate it directly. Secure limits transport, SameSite limits cross-site sending, and Max-Age controls lifetime; none of those hides the value from same-origin script.

facts.title: Security headers reduce impact; they do not fix the underlying bug
facts.fact: Security response headers change browser behaviour around content the application already serves, so they reduce impact rather than remove vulnerabilities. Content-Security-Policy restricts script, style and frame sources; Strict-Transport-Security forces HTTPS for future requests; X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops MIME sniffing; Referrer-Policy limits URL leakage; frame-ancestors controls embedding. HSTS is ignored when delivered over plain HTTP, and a CSP containing 'unsafe-inline' or a broad script-src host list provides little protection.
details: Send headers on error and API responses too; frameworks often add them only on successful HTML responses.
Start CSP in report-only mode, collect violations, then enforce; a policy that breaks the app tends to be removed entirely.
Headers do not replace authorization, parameterisation or output encoding.

configs.purpose: Apply a baseline header set to every response, including errors, with a CSP that blocks inline and plugin content.

mcqs.question: Under which condition does a browser honour Strict-Transport-Security?
options: Only when the header arrives over an HTTPS connection
Whenever the header appears in any HTTP response
Only for requests that already use HTTP/2
Only when the cookie is marked Secure
mcqs.rationale: The HSTS header is ignored on plain HTTP, which is why the first request must already be protected or redirected at the network edge. The other options do not gate HSTS processing.

facts.title: Password storage needs a slow, salted, memory-hard KDF
facts.fact: Password storage requires a deliberately slow, salted key-derivation function so that a stolen database cannot be cracked cheaply. Argon2id is the first choice, with bcrypt, scrypt or PBKDF2 as acceptable alternatives when the platform lacks it; each password gets a unique random salt, and the cost is tuned so one verification takes a noticeable fraction of a second. General-purpose digests such as SHA-256, SHA-1 and MD5 are built for speed and are unsuitable even with a salt, because GPUs test billions of candidates per second.
details: OWASP's published baseline at the time of writing: Argon2id with m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1; bcrypt with cost 10 or more; PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600000 iterations. Recheck the current guidance before fixing parameters in code.
bcrypt truncates at 72 bytes; reject or carefully pre-hash longer secrets and never truncate silently.
Store the algorithm and parameters alongside the hash so cost can be raised and old hashes rehashed on the next successful login.

code.issue: SHA-256 is designed for speed, so offline guessing is cheap and identical passwords collide. Argon2id salts each hash and makes each guess memory-hard; verify with the library's constant-time check and rehash when parameters change.

mcqs.question: Why is a salted SHA-256 hash still a poor choice for passwords?
options: The digest is fast, so an attacker can test a very large number of candidates
A salt makes identical passwords produce identical hashes
SHA-256 cannot represent long passwords
The salt must be stored in the cookie
mcqs.rationale: Salt defeats precomputed tables and hides duplicate passwords, but it does not slow each guess. Password KDFs deliberately consume CPU and memory to make guessing expensive.

misconceptions.claim: Adding a salt makes any password hash safe.
misconceptions.correction: A salt prevents rainbow tables and stops two users with the same password from sharing a hash, but a fast digest still allows billions of guesses per second. The work factor, not the salt alone, is what makes cracking expensive.

CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort

facts.title: Authentication answers who; authorization answers what, per request
facts.fact: Authentication establishes the identity behind a request; authorization decides whether that identity may perform this action on this resource. A valid token proves only the first, so every endpoint must evaluate permission for the specific object and operation on the server. Return 401 when credentials are missing or invalid and 403 when the identity is known but not permitted; for object lookups, 404 can avoid confirming that a resource exists.
details: Client-side route guards and hidden buttons are usability features; an attacker calls the API directly.
Check function-level authorization (may this role call this endpoint?) and object-level authorization (may this subject use this row?).
Deny by default: an endpoint with no explicit policy should fail closed rather than inherit allow.

mcqs.question: A request carries a valid session token for a normal user who asks for another user's invoice. Which control should reject it?
options: Object-level authorization in the invoice handler
Authentication middleware, because the token is invalid
The browser's CORS policy
TLS client certificate verification
mcqs.rationale: The token is valid, so authentication succeeds; the missing control is whether this subject may access this object. CORS limits browser reads, not server-side access, and TLS proves the channel rather than the user's rights.

facts.title: BOLA/IDOR: scope every object lookup to the caller
facts.fact: Broken object level authorization (BOLA, also called IDOR) appears when an endpoint accepts an object identifier and returns or modifies the object without checking that the caller owns or may access it. Authentication is not enough: the request is valid, the user is real, and the identifier is simply changed. The fix is to make the subject part of the query, for example filtering by owner id, and to return 404 rather than 403 when the row is not visible so the endpoint does not confirm existence.
details: Apply the same rule to nested routes such as /users/{uid}/orders/{oid}; checking the outer id is not enough.
Unguessable identifiers raise the cost of enumeration but are not an authorization control.
Use one server-side policy function for read, update and delete so the checks cannot drift apart.

code.issue: Authentication proves who is calling but not that they own the row; the secure query makes ownership part of the lookup. Returning 404 avoids telling an attacker whether the identifier exists.

mcqs.question: Which change most directly fixes an IDOR in GET /orders/{id}?
options: Add the authenticated customer id to the database filter
Switch the identifier from an integer to a UUID
Require HTTPS for the endpoint
Return 403 for every failed lookup
mcqs.rationale: The missing control is an ownership predicate in the query. UUIDs only slow enumeration, TLS protects transport, and 403 can still confirm existence without fixing access.

facts.title: Validate with a closed schema before business logic runs
facts.fact: Input validation constrains data to the shape the business logic expects: type, length, range, format, character set and required fields. Prefer an allowlist expressed as a schema, reject unknown fields, and decode or canonicalise once before validating so encoded variants cannot slip past. Validation reduces attack surface and catches mistakes, but it is not a substitute for output encoding or parameterisation, because a value that is valid for the business can still be dangerous in a different interpreter.
details: Validate on the server even when the client validates; the client is under attacker control.
Use structured parsers for JSON, XML and multipart bodies rather than regular expressions over the whole document.
Bound collection sizes and nesting depth to avoid resource exhaustion.

code.secure:
# SECURE: bounded types and unknown fields rejected
class Profile(BaseModel):
    display_name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80, pattern=r"^[\w .-]+$")
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
code.issue: Allowing extra keys lets a client smuggle fields into later binding steps, and an unbounded string gives no length guarantee. A closed model with a bounded pattern fails early and predictably.

mcqs.question: What is the main reason to reject unknown JSON fields in a request schema?
options: It prevents unintended fields from reaching binding or persistence layers
It makes the response smaller
It removes the need for authorization checks
It guarantees the data is safe to render as HTML
mcqs.rationale: Closed schemas stop parameter smuggling and mass assignment. They do not replace authorization or output encoding, and response size is unrelated.

references.title: OWASP Proactive Controls: C5 Validate All Inputs

facts.title: Secure defaults fail closed and are safe without extra configuration
facts.fact: A secure default is the behaviour a developer gets without opting in: deny by default, TLS required, debug output off, no built-in accounts, cookies marked Secure and HttpOnly, and least-privilege service identities. Defaults matter because most deployments never revisit them. Framework templates can undermine this: django-admin startproject writes DEBUG = True into settings, and with DEBUG = False an empty ALLOWED_HOSTS rejects every request, so production configuration must be explicit rather than assumed.
details: Flask leaves debug off unless app.run(debug=True) or FLASK_DEBUG=1 is set; never enable it in a deployed process.
Express includes stack traces in its default error handler unless NODE_ENV is production, and a custom handler can reintroduce leakage.
Add a startup check that refuses to boot with debug on, a default secret, or wildcard CORS in production.

configs.snippet:
DEBUG = False
ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["app.example.internal"]
SECRET_KEY = os.environ["DJANGO_SECRET_KEY"]
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
configs.purpose: Replace development defaults with an explicit production posture: no debug, named hosts, injected key and HTTPS-only cookies.

mcqs.question: A Django project generated by startproject is deployed unchanged with DEBUG still True. What is the main risk?
options: Detailed exception pages and settings can be exposed to users
The database driver stops accepting parameters
CSRF protection is disabled for all views
Session cookies stop being signed
mcqs.rationale: DEBUG=True enables verbose error pages that can reveal source, settings and SQL. It does not disable parameterisation, CSRF middleware or cookie signing.

misconceptions.claim: Framework defaults are production-safe because the framework is mature.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults favour development convenience. Django's generated settings enable DEBUG and leave ALLOWED_HOSTS empty, Flask can be started with debug on, and many stacks default to permissive CORS or bind to all interfaces. Production posture has to be chosen and tested.

facts.title: CSRF exploits ambient credentials; tokens bind the request to the session
facts.fact: Cross-site request forgery works because browsers attach a site's cookies to requests initiated by another site, so an attacker's page can trigger a state change as the victim. Defences bind the request to something the attacker cannot read or guess: a per-session synchronizer token, a signed double-submit cookie, or an Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check. State-changing operations must not be reachable by GET, and the token must be verified on the server before the action rather than merely rendered in the form.
details: Login and logout are state-changing too; login CSRF can bind a victim to an attacker's account.
For JSON APIs, require a custom header or a token in a header, because simple cross-origin form posts cannot set arbitrary headers.
The Express csurf package was deprecated in 2022; choose a maintained alternative or implement the pattern explicitly.

code.secure:
# SECURE: Flask-WTF checks a per-session token on state-changing requests
from flask_wtf.csrf import CSRFProtect

csrf = CSRFProtect(app)

@app.post('/account/email')
def change_email():
    current_user.email = request.form['email']
    db.session.commit()
    return 'ok'
code.issue: Without a token, any site can submit the form with the victim's cookies. CSRFProtect rejects unsafe methods that lack a valid token; the form template must render csrf_token() so the legitimate request carries it.

mcqs.question: Why does a synchronizer token stop CSRF?
options: The attacker's site cannot read the victim's token to include it in the forged request
The token encrypts the request body
The token replaces the session cookie
The token makes the request idempotent
mcqs.rationale: Same-origin policy prevents the attacker from reading the token, so a cross-site request can carry cookies but not a matching token. The token does not encrypt data or replace the session.

references.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

facts.title: SameSite is a browser default, not a complete CSRF control
facts.fact: SameSite tells the browser when to attach a cookie to a cross-site request. Lax, the default in Chromium since version 80, sends the cookie on top-level safe navigations such as link clicks but not on cross-site POSTs; Strict withholds it on inbound navigation, which can make links appear logged out; None sends it everywhere and requires Secure. None of these settings is a complete CSRF defence, because Lax still permits top-level GET requests and older or non-browser clients may ignore the attribute.
details: Chromium applies a short 'Lax plus POST' exception to cookies set within the last two minutes, so a freshly issued cookie can still accompany a cross-site POST.
Same-site is broader than same-origin: sibling subdomains count as the same site, so a compromised subdomain can still send cookies.
Pair SameSite with token or Origin validation on state-changing endpoints.

configs.snippet:
Set-Cookie: sid=REDACTED; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: __Host-csrf=REDACTED; Path=/; Secure; SameSite=Strict
configs.purpose: Send the session cookie on top-level navigation but keep the CSRF cookie strict, and scope the CSRF cookie to the exact host.

mcqs.question: Which request still carries a SameSite=Lax cookie cross-site in current browsers?
options: A top-level navigation caused by clicking a link
A cross-site form POST
A cross-site fetch from JavaScript
A cross-site iframe load
mcqs.rationale: Lax allows top-level safe navigations such as link clicks. Cross-site POSTs, subresource fetches and iframes are excluded, which is why Lax alone does not stop every CSRF vector.

misconceptions.claim: Setting SameSite=Strict makes CSRF impossible and removes the need for tokens.
misconceptions.correction: Strict stops the cookie on cross-site requests, but it also breaks legitimate inbound links, so teams often relax it. Browser exceptions, same-site subdomains and non-browser clients mean server-side token or Origin checks are still needed for state changes.

references.title: Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

facts.title: Resolve and confine file paths; never trust a client-supplied name
facts.fact: Path traversal arises when a client-supplied name is joined to a base directory without confinement, so ../ sequences, an absolute path, encoded separators or a symlink escape the intended tree. os.path.join('/srv/reports', '/etc/passwd') returns '/etc/passwd' because an absolute second argument discards the base. The robust fix is to avoid client filenames entirely, mapping opaque identifiers to stored names, or to resolve the final path and verify it is inside the resolved base before opening it.
details: Decode URL and filesystem encodings before the containment check; do not check the raw string and then decode it for use.
Path.resolve() follows symlinks, so containment of the resolved target also covers symlink escapes, though the check and open still need race protection.
Reject NUL bytes and empty names, and normalise case on case-insensitive filesystems.

code.issue: The vulnerable version accepts ../../ and absolute paths. Resolving first and comparing against the resolved base rejects both, and covers symlink targets; an identifier-to-filename map avoids the problem altogether.

mcqs.question: Which input defeats os.path.join('/srv/reports', name)?
options: A value starting with a path separator
A value longer than 255 bytes
A value containing a space
A value with a Unicode letter
mcqs.rationale: On POSIX, an absolute second argument discards the earlier components, so the result points wherever the input names. Length, spaces and Unicode do not by themselves escape the base.

references.title: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

facts.title: A secret in source control is compromised, even after deletion
facts.fact: A secret committed to source control should be treated as compromised, because history, forks, caches and CI logs retain it after the line is deleted. Environment variables are an improvement over literals but are still readable by the process, child processes, crash dumps and anyone with host access. Use a secret manager or workload identity to issue short-lived credentials, keep secrets out of build arguments and image layers, and run secret scanning in pre-commit and CI with rotation as the response to a finding.
details: Add .env and key material to .gitignore before the first commit; ignoring later does not remove history.
Docker ARG values are visible in image history; use BuildKit secret mounts instead.
Scope secrets per environment and per service, and log access to the secret store.

configs.snippet:
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
    with:
      role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::000000000000:role/deploy
      aws-region: eu-west-1
configs.purpose: Exchange a short-lived OpenID Connect identity for cloud credentials instead of storing a long-lived access key in CI.

mcqs.question: A live API key was committed and then deleted in a later commit. What is the correct first response?
options: Revoke and rotate the key, then purge it from history where feasible
Delete the branch and assume the key is gone
Add the file to .gitignore
Rewrite the commit message to remove the key name
mcqs.rationale: The key remains in history, clones and caches, so revocation is the only reliable containment. Ignoring the file or rewriting messages does not remove the exposed value.

facts.title: API keys identify a client application, not a person
facts.fact: An API key is a long-lived shared secret that identifies a client application, not a human user, and it usually carries no fine-grained subject context. If the key is embedded in a browser bundle or mobile binary it is extractable, so it cannot protect user-specific data on its own. Treat keys as bearer credentials: scope them narrowly, hash them at rest, allow rotation with overlap, send them in an Authorization or dedicated header, and never in a query string where logs, proxies and Referer headers capture them.
details: Use separate keys per environment and per integration; a leaked test key should not open production.
Detect leaked keys in public repositories and rotate automatically rather than relying on revocation after abuse.
For user-delegated access, use OAuth scopes and short-lived tokens instead of a shared key.

configs.snippet:
GET /v1/reports HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.internal
Authorization: Bearer REDACTED_API_KEY
configs.purpose: Carry the key in a request header so it stays out of URLs, access logs and browser Referer values.

mcqs.question: A single-page application needs to call an API on behalf of a signed-in user. Why is a static API key embedded in the bundle the wrong design?
options: Any visitor can extract the key, and it does not represent the user's own permissions
API keys cannot be sent over TLS
API keys are always longer than JWTs
Browsers block the Authorization header on same-origin requests
mcqs.rationale: The bundle is public, so the key is public; and a client-level secret cannot express per-user authorization. Use a user-delegated flow with short-lived tokens instead.

misconceptions.claim: An API key authenticates the end user.
misconceptions.correction: An API key authenticates the calling application and often only proves that some client was issued a key. It carries no user identity, so per-user authorization still requires a user authentication and consent flow.

facts.title: Framing control belongs in a response header, not JavaScript
facts.fact: Clickjacking loads a sensitive page in a transparent or disguised frame and tricks the user into clicking controls they cannot see. The reliable control is a response header: Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors 'none' (or an explicit list) is checked by modern browsers, while X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN remains as a legacy fallback. JavaScript frame-busting is not dependable because it can be blocked or bypassed, and it fails when scripting is disabled.
details: frame-ancestors supersedes X-Frame-Options in browsers that support CSP; sending both is harmless and covers older clients.
Apply the policy to every sensitive response, including error pages and JSON that could be framed.
Where embedding is a product requirement, list exact ancestors rather than allowing all origins.

configs.snippet:
add_header Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'none'" always;
add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;
configs.purpose: Stop the browser from rendering the application inside any frame, with a legacy header for older clients.

mcqs.question: Which control reliably prevents a page from being framed by another origin?
options: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
A JavaScript window.top check
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
SameSite=Strict on the session cookie
mcqs.rationale: frame-ancestors is enforced by the browser's frame loading logic. Script checks can be bypassed or disabled, nosniff affects MIME handling, and SameSite affects cookie sending rather than framing.

misconceptions.claim: A framebusting script is equivalent to a frame-ancestors policy.
misconceptions.correction: Framebusting runs after the document loads, can be neutralised by sandboxing or scripting restrictions, and fails closed only if implemented very carefully. A header is enforced before rendering.

references.title: CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames

facts.title: NoSQL injection often arrives as a JSON object, not a string
facts.fact: Document databases accept structured filters, so injection can happen without a quote or a comment: a request body such as an object where a string was expected can introduce operators like $ne, $gt, $regex or $where. If the application passes parsed JSON straight into a query, the attacker controls the shape of the predicate and can match records they should not see. The fix is to extract scalar values, assert their types, build the filter explicitly, and reject keys beginning with $ or containing dots.
details: Type confusion matters: an array where a string is expected may match any of several values.
$where executes JavaScript on the server and should be disabled or never reachable from user input.
Schema validation at the edge is useful, but the query builder should still refuse operator objects.

code.issue: Passing the body directly lets an object replace the equality test with an operator. Casting to string and constructing an explicit filter removes operator injection; the password check then uses a real verifier rather than a database match.

mcqs.question: Why is passing req.body directly to a MongoDB findOne dangerous?
options: Object keys can be interpreted as query operators
MongoDB cannot store strings longer than 255 bytes
JSON bodies are always parsed as JavaScript
findOne disables TLS for the query
mcqs.rationale: MongoDB treats keys such as $ne and $gt as operators, so an object-shaped value changes the predicate. The other statements are false: BSON supports long strings, JSON is data, and TLS is unrelated to query shape.

references.title: CWE-943: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic

facts.title: Pass argument vectors, not shell strings, to child processes
facts.fact: Command injection occurs when untrusted data reaches a shell interpreter, so characters that mean something to the shell become part of the command. In Python, subprocess.run(..., shell=True) and os.system parse a string; in Node.js, child_process.exec does the same, while execFile and spawn with an argument array do not. The structural fix is to invoke the program directly with separate arguments and no shell, then validate the argument values against a narrow allowlist and drop unnecessary privileges.
details: shlex.quote() helps in a few POSIX shells but is easy to misuse across platforms; removing the shell is more reliable.
Never build a command from a request field when a library call can do the job.
Run the child with a minimal environment, a timeout and a working directory that the service can write only when necessary.

code.secure:
# SECURE: argv list, no shell, and a validated address
import ipaddress
import subprocess

def ping(host: str) -> str:
    ipaddress.ip_address(host)          # reject anything that is not an address
    return subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False,
                          capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=5).stdout
code.issue: With shell=True the host value can introduce additional commands; with an argv list the value is a single argument. Validation narrows input, but removing the shell is what eliminates the second parser.

mcqs.question: Which Node.js call avoids shell interpretation by default?
options: child_process.execFile
child_process.exec
child_process.execSync with a string
eval
mcqs.rationale: execFile runs the named program with an argument array and does not use a shell unless shell:true is set. exec and execSync with a string go through a shell, and eval is unrelated to process execution but equally unsafe for untrusted input.

references.title: OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet
CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command

facts.title: User input must be template data, never template source
facts.fact: Server-side template injection happens when an application compiles user input as a template instead of passing it as a variable. Template engines evaluate expressions with access to the context object, so ordinary autoescaping does not help: escaping protects the output of a template, not the template program itself. Use a fixed template file and pass request values as context, and if user-authored templates are a genuine product requirement, use a logic-less engine, a restricted context and a sandbox as defence in depth rather than as the only boundary.
details: render_template_string in Flask and Template(...).render in other engines compile their argument; prefer render_template with a fixed name.
The context is part of the attack surface: exposing settings, database objects or framework globals supplies the primitives an escape needs.
Error messages that echo the compiled expression can confirm template evaluation during review.

code.issue: render_template_string compiles its argument, so template syntax in name is evaluated with the application's context. Passing the value as a context variable keeps it outside the template program.

mcqs.question: Why does Jinja2 autoescaping not prevent SSTI?
options: Autoescaping applies to rendered output, while the injected string is compiled as template code
Jinja2 disables autoescaping for all templates
Autoescaping only escapes numbers
The template engine evaluates output before escaping it
mcqs.rationale: The dangerous transition is compiling attacker text into template code; escaping happens later when that code produces output. The other statements misdescribe how autoescaping works.

references.title: CWE-1336: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine

facts.title: SSRF: validate the destination after resolution, not just the string
facts.fact: Server-side request forgery occurs when an application fetches a URL supplied by a user, letting the attacker use the server's network position to reach internal services, cloud metadata endpoints or loopback-only administration interfaces. A blocklist of hostname strings is weak: decimal, octal and IPv6 forms, redirects and DNS rebinding all change where the request lands after the check. Restrict the scheme and port, resolve the host and reject non-global addresses, pin the resolved address for the connection, and disable redirects so the validated destination is the one actually contacted.
details: ipaddress.ip_address(...).is_global is a useful predicate, but handle IPv4-mapped IPv6 and parse the literal exactly as the HTTP client will.
Metadata services commonly live on link-local addresses; block them at the network layer as well as in code.
A URL allowlist of exact hosts is stronger than a denylist, but still needs redirect and DNS handling.

code.issue: The check must happen on the resolved address and redirects must not silently re-target the request. Even then, a second DNS answer at connect time can differ, so egress policy remains the stronger control.

mcqs.question: Why is a hostname denylist insufficient for SSRF protection?
options: The hostname can resolve differently at check time and connect time, and redirects can change the destination
DNS cannot return private addresses
HTTPS forbids requests to internal hosts
URL parsers reject non-ASCII hostnames
mcqs.rationale: DNS rebinding and redirects defeat a one-time string check; the request may land somewhere the check never saw. DNS can return private addresses, HTTPS does not restrict destinations, and parser behaviour varies rather than protecting you.

facts.title: Uploads: trust the content you decode, not the filename or MIME type
facts.fact: Every part of an upload is attacker-controlled: the filename, the declared Content-Type, the extension and the bytes themselves. Storing the original name under a served directory enables path traversal, overwrites and content-type confusion, while trusting the declared type lets an executable or HTML document through. Use server-generated names, an extension allowlist, content inspection or re-encoding, a size limit, storage outside the web root or in object storage, and a download response that forces attachment with nosniff.
details: Image decoders are themselves attack surface; re-encode to a simple format and strip metadata rather than serving the original.
Polyglot files can be valid in two formats, so extension checks alone are insufficient without content handling.
Store uploads on a separate hostname or bucket so a stored HTML file cannot run in the application origin.

code.secure:
# SECURE: server-generated name, size cap, decoded image, non-executable store
import os
import uuid
from PIL import Image

@app.post('/avatar')
def upload():
    f = request.files['file']
    if request.content_length > 2 * 1024 * 1024:
        abort(413)
    img = Image.open(f.stream)
    img.verify()
    f.stream.seek(0)
    img = Image.open(f.stream)
    img.thumbnail((512, 512))
    name = f"{uuid.uuid4().hex}.png"
    img.save(os.path.join('/srv/media', name))
    return {'name': name}
code.issue: The vulnerable path accepts traversal in the filename and executes whatever type is stored. A generated name, a decoded image and a non-served directory remove both the path and the execution primitives; the declared Content-Type is never trusted.

mcqs.question: Which control best stops an uploaded .php file from executing?
options: Store uploads outside the web root and serve them through a handler that forces download
Check that the Content-Type header says image/png
Rename the file but keep the extension
Limit the upload to 1 MB
mcqs.rationale: Execution depends on where and how the file is served; removing it from the executable document root is structural. The Content-Type header is client-controlled, renaming alone does not change handling, and size limits do not affect type.

misconceptions.claim: Validating the Content-Type header is enough to make uploads safe.
misconceptions.correction: The client sets that header and can claim image/png for any bytes. Inspect or re-encode the content, constrain the stored name and location, and control how the file is served.

facts.title: Deserialising untrusted bytes can execute code
facts.fact: Many serialisation formats can reconstruct objects, not just data, and object reconstruction runs attacker-influenced constructors or callbacks. Python's pickle can call arbitrary callables during load, YAML has unsafe loaders, PHP unserialize can instantiate classes and trigger magic methods, and Java ObjectInputStream is the root of many gadget chains. Accept JSON or another data-only format with a strict schema, use yaml.safe_load for YAML, and never deserialise a blob from a client even if it is signed by a party you think you trust.
details: A signature proves who sent the bytes, not that the bytes are safe to deserialise; a compromised or over-privileged sender still yields code execution.
In Python, prefer JSON plus pydantic or dataclasses; for YAML, safe_load returns only basic types.
If a binary format is unavoidable, isolate the parser in a low-privilege process and validate the resulting object graph.

code.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE (illustrative): pickle executes constructors while loading
import pickle

def load_prefs(raw: bytes) -> dict:
    return pickle.loads(raw)          # raw comes from a request cookie
code.issue: pickle reconstructs arbitrary classes and can invoke attacker-chosen callables; JSON plus a closed schema only ever produces plain data. Signing the pickle would not make loading it safe.

mcqs.question: Which statement about signed pickle payloads is correct?
options: A valid signature does not make deserialisation safe
Signing removes the need for input validation
pickle refuses to load untrusted classes automatically
HMAC turns pickle into a data-only format
mcqs.rationale: Verification answers who produced the bytes; loading them still executes object reconstruction. HMAC adds integrity, not a safe object model.

facts.title: Open redirects turn your domain into a phishing and OAuth bypass tool
facts.fact: An open redirect takes a destination from the request and sends the browser there without constraining it, so attackers can present a trusted link that lands on a phishing page. The same primitive can defeat OAuth redirect URI checks when an identity provider has registered a redirector. Allow only relative paths on the current host, or compare the resolved destination against an exact host allowlist, and reject scheme-relative forms, backslashes, userinfo and encoded variants.
details: Parse with a real URL library and compare the final scheme and host; do not rely on startswith or a substring check.
Browsers normalise some backslash and whitespace forms, so validate the same way the browser will interpret the value.
Django's url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme implements the common same-host check; use a maintained helper rather than rolling your own.

code.issue: The vulnerable handler forwards to whatever the parameter names. Resolving against a fixed base and comparing scheme and host constrains the destination; backslash rejection covers browser normalisation quirks.

mcqs.question: Which validation is appropriate for a post-login redirect target?
options: Resolve it and require the same scheme and host as the application
Require that it starts with a slash
Require that it does not contain the word http
URL-encode the target before redirecting
mcqs.rationale: A leading slash does not exclude protocol-relative //host values, and string filters miss encodings. Comparing the resolved scheme and host is the reliable check.

references.title: Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet
CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site

facts.title: Reflecting arbitrary origins with credentials exposes authenticated APIs
facts.fact: CORS is a browser-side rule that decides whether a cross-origin script may read a response; it is not server-side authorization. Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * combined with credentials is rejected by browsers, but reflecting the request's Origin and setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true lets any site read authenticated responses. Configure an exact origin allowlist, send Vary: Origin so shared caches do not mix responses, and remember that non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely.
details: Preflight requests only gate non-simple methods and headers; a simple cross-origin POST is sent even if the response cannot be read.
Subdomain wildcards trust every subdomain, including ones that host user content or have been taken over.
Credentials include cookies and TLS client certificates; omit them unless the flow genuinely needs cross-origin authenticated reads.

code.vulnerable:
// VULNERABLE (illustrative): any origin is reflected with credentials
app.use(cors({ origin: true, credentials: true }));
code.issue: origin: true reflects whatever the caller sends, so every site can read credentialed responses. The allowlist limits the header to known front ends; the cors middleware also emits Vary: Origin for cache correctness.

mcqs.question: What does Access-Control-Allow-Origin actually control?
options: Whether browser JavaScript from another origin may read the response
Whether the server accepts the request at all
Whether cookies are signed
Whether TLS is required
mcqs.rationale: The browser sends many cross-origin requests regardless and uses CORS to decide whether to expose the response to script. CORS is not authentication, cookie integrity or transport security.

misconceptions.claim: A restrictive CORS policy protects the API from unauthorized callers.
misconceptions.correction: CORS only constrains browser-based reads. curl, server-side scripts and native apps ignore it, and simple requests still reach the server. Authorization must be enforced on every request regardless of origin.

facts.title: Rotate the session identifier when privilege changes
facts.fact: If a session identifier issued before authentication remains valid after login, an attacker who planted or observed that identifier shares the authenticated session. This is session fixation, and it survives password changes and role upgrades unless the server explicitly rotates the identifier and invalidates the old one. Rotate on login, logout, privilege change and password reset, keep sessions server-side with idle and absolute timeouts, and never accept a session identifier from a URL parameter.
details: Flask's default session is a signed client-side cookie; session.clear() before setting the user id prevents an old cookie from carrying the new identity.
Server-side stores should delete the old record rather than merely stop referencing it, so a stolen copy cannot be replayed.
Bind sessions to a coarse client context where appropriate, but avoid breaking mobile users who change networks.

code.issue: The vulnerable handler upgrades an existing session in place, so a pre-planted identifier becomes authenticated. Clearing the session before storing the identity forces a new identifier and invalidates the old state.

mcqs.question: When must a session identifier be rotated?
options: On login, logout, privilege change and password reset
Only when the user changes browser
Only on the first request of a day
Never, because rotation breaks CSRF tokens
mcqs.rationale: Those events change the security context, so a pre-existing identifier must not carry the new privileges. Rotating at other arbitrary times is optional; CSRF tokens can be reissued with the session.

facts.title: Rate limit by identity and action, and share the counter across instances
facts.fact: Rate limiting bounds how often a client can attempt an action, which reduces password guessing, OTP brute force, scraping and resource exhaustion. Limiting only by source IP fails behind carrier NAT and is easily distributed across botnets, so combine account, token, IP and endpoint dimensions, and use a shared store such as Redis so every instance sees the same counter. Return 429 with Retry-After, prefer short delays over permanent account lockout, and trust forwarded IP headers only from known proxies.
details: Login, OTP verification, password reset, invitation acceptance and data export deserve separate, tighter budgets.
A token bucket allows short bursts while enforcing a sustained rate; a fixed window at the boundary can double the effective rate.
Rate limiting complements, but does not replace, strong password storage, MFA and anomaly detection.

configs.purpose: Apply a coarse per-IP ceiling at the edge; the application should also count per account and per endpoint in a shared store.

mcqs.question: Why is per-IP rate limiting alone weak for login protection?
options: Attackers can distribute attempts across many addresses, and NAT hides many users behind one address
IP addresses change too rarely to matter
Rate limiting only works for GET requests
Browsers ignore 429 responses
mcqs.rationale: Distributed guessing spreads attempts across sources, while NAT causes collateral lockout. Add per-account and per-token budgets, and keep a global ceiling.

facts.title: Check-then-use races on the filesystem need one atomic operation
facts.fact: A time-of-check to time-of-use race occurs when a program verifies a condition and later acts on it, with a window in which an attacker changes the object. Classic examples are os.path.exists() followed by open(), os.access() followed by open(), and writing to a path that can be replaced by a symlink. Perform the check and the use in one operation: create with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, refuse symlinks with O_NOFOLLOW, operate on the returned file descriptor, and verify ownership with fstat rather than by path.
details: Opening a directory with O_DIRECTORY and using openat-style relative operations narrows the window further.
Temp files should come from tempfile with secure defaults rather than a predictable name in a shared directory.
Race conditions also affect databases and business logic; the same principle applies: make the decision and the write atomic.

code.vulnerable:
# VULNERABLE (illustrative): a symlink can appear between check and open
import os

def write_upload(path: str, data: bytes) -> None:
    if os.path.exists(path):
        raise FileExistsError(path)
    with open(path, 'wb') as fh:
        fh.write(data)
code.secure:
# SECURE: exclusive create, no symlink following, single atomic open
import os

def write_upload(path: str, data: bytes) -> None:
    flags = os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | getattr(os, 'O_NOFOLLOW', 0)
    fd = os.open(path, flags, 0o600)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, 'wb') as fh:
            fh.write(data)
    except BaseException:
        os.unlink(path)
        raise
code.issue: The exists/open pair is two syscalls, so another process can insert a symlink in between. O_EXCL and O_NOFOLLOW make creation itself the check; containment within the intended directory still has to be enforced separately.

mcqs.question: Which primitive removes the check-then-open race for a new file?
options: os.open with O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW
os.path.exists followed by open
os.access followed by open
A random filename generated by the client
mcqs.rationale: O_EXCL makes creation fail if the name exists, and O_NOFOLLOW refuses a symlink at the final component, in the same syscall. Separate checks leave a window, and client-chosen names are attacker-controlled.

facts.title: Bind only the fields a client is allowed to set
facts.fact: Mass assignment occurs when an API maps request fields onto a model or object without restricting which fields are writable. A client can then set attributes the UI never showed, such as role, is_admin, owner_id, balance or verified. Fix it with an explicit input model that lists client-writable fields, rejects unknown keys, and marks server-owned fields read-only; derive privileged values from the authenticated principal rather than from the request body.
details: An allowlist is safer than a blocklist because new sensitive columns are protected by default.
Django REST Framework serializers and pydantic models both support explicit field sets and read-only fields.
Audit nested objects and bulk endpoints too: a permitted parent field can hide an unrestricted child mapping.

code.issue: Generic binding lets a client write server-owned columns; the closed model makes privilege fields unrepresentable. The handler must also verify that uid belongs to the caller.

mcqs.question: A profile update endpoint accepts a JSON body and copies every key onto the user object. What is the direct risk?
options: A client can set fields such as role or is_admin
The response will be cached incorrectly
CSRF tokens stop working
TLS session resumption fails
mcqs.rationale: Unrestricted binding turns every column into a client-writable field, enabling privilege escalation or data forgery. Caching, CSRF and TLS are unrelated to the binding step.

references.title: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes
API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization

facts.title: Scope the lookup to the caller and project explicit response fields
facts.fact: Excessive data exposure happens when an endpoint returns more of an object than the caller needs, often because it serialises an ORM row or a generic dictionary. It usually compounds with broken object-level authorization: a lookup keyed only on the path id lets any authenticated caller name someone else's record, and an over-broad serializer then hands over that record's password hash, internal identifiers, feature flags or moderation notes. Scope the query to the subject (owner or tenant) and return an explicit response model with a separate projection for each audience, and apply the same discipline to error messages and nested relations.
details: Framework defaults differ: many serialisers include every column unless fields or exclude are set.
Put the subject in the query: filter on owner_id or tenant_id so another user's row does not match, instead of fetching by id and checking afterwards.
Answer 404 for rows outside the caller's scope so the endpoint does not confirm that another user's object exists.
GraphQL resolvers need field-level authorization, because the client chooses which fields to request.
Truncate or redact identifiers that are not needed; internal ids can enable enumeration or cross-tenant references.

code.issue: The lookup is keyed only on the caller-supplied id, so any authenticated user can read any account (BOLA/IDOR); echoing every column adds excessive data exposure, sending owner ids, routing numbers and internal risk flags to the wrong person. Scoping the query to the subject and returning an explicit projection fix different flaws, and neither substitutes for the other.

mcqs.question: Which practice most directly prevents accidental exposure of new database columns?
options: Returning an explicit response model with named fields
Returning the ORM object and relying on the client to ignore extra fields
Renaming the columns to obscure names
Compressing the JSON response
mcqs.rationale: An allowlist projection fails closed when a column is added, whereas whole-object serialisation automatically exposes it. Obscure names and compression provide no access control.

references.title: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

facts.title: Never let the token choose its own verification algorithm
facts.fact: A JWT header carries an alg field, and verification is only safe if the verifier decides which algorithms and keys it accepts. Trusting the header enables the none algorithm and algorithm-confusion attacks, where a token signed with HMAC is checked using an RSA public key as the HMAC secret. Pin the algorithm set, select the key by trusted issuer and key id rather than by header-supplied material, and reject none outright; PyJWT 2.x refuses to decode without an explicit algorithms argument, but older releases did not.
details: Use separate verification paths when an issuer genuinely supports more than one algorithm, rather than one generic decoder.
Check that the key type matches the algorithm; an RSA key must never be used as an HMAC secret.
Keep the libraries patched: algorithm-confusion handling has changed across major versions.

code.issue: Reading alg from the unverified header lets an attacker request none or HMAC verification with a public key. Pinning RS256 and the matching key blocks both, and require closes missing-claim gaps.

mcqs.question: In an algorithm-confusion attack on RS256, what does the attacker exploit?
options: The verifier accepts HS256 and uses the RSA public key as the HMAC secret
RSA private keys are mathematically predictable
The JWT payload is not base64url encoded
TLS strips the signature before the application sees it
mcqs.rationale: A public key is public, so if the verifier treats it as an HMAC secret the attacker can compute a valid MAC. Pinning the algorithm and key type prevents the substitution.

misconceptions.claim: A JWT library verifies signatures safely by default, whatever algorithm the token names.
misconceptions.correction: Many historical libraries honoured the header or accepted none; modern releases often require an explicit algorithm list. Safe verification is a configuration decision, not something to assume from the library name.

references.title: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

facts.title: A valid signature does not make the claims valid for you
facts.fact: Signature verification proves that a token was issued by someone holding the key; it does not prove that the token is current or intended for this service. Validate exp and nbf, require an expiry rather than treating a missing one as infinite, and check aud and iss against exact expected values. PyJWT validates exp and nbf when present and checks aud and iss only when you pass audience and issuer, so an explicit require list is needed to reject tokens that omit them.
details: Allow only a small clock skew, such as 30 seconds, and keep server clocks synchronised.
Reject tokens whose aud does not include this service; a token minted for another internal API should not be accepted.
For revocation-sensitive operations, combine short lifetimes with a server-side session or token version check.

code.issue: Without audience and issuer parameters, a token minted for a different service can pass, and a token with no exp is accepted. options.require rejects missing claims, and leeway tolerates small clock differences.

mcqs.question: Which claim check prevents a token issued for service A from being accepted by service B?
options: audience
nbf
iat
jti
mcqs.rationale: aud names the intended recipient, so B must reject a token whose aud does not include B. nbf and iat constrain time, and jti identifies a token but does not express audience.

references.title: RFC 7519: JSON Web Token (JWT), sections 4.1 and 7.2
PyJWT usage: reading and validating claims

facts.title: The kid header is a lookup hint, not a path or a query fragment
facts.fact: The kid header tells the verifier which key to use, but the token is still unverified when that value is read. If an application interpolates kid into a file path or SQL query, or fetches whatever key kid names, the header becomes an injection primitive or lets the attacker select a key they control. Treat kid as an index into a fixed, trusted key set, reject unknown values, and validate that the selected key's type, use and algorithm match the expected verification path.
details: Key rotation needs old and new keys to coexist for a bounded overlap, but only keys from the trusted set are eligible.
Bound the number of cached keys so a stream of unknown kid values cannot exhaust memory.
Log unknown kid values as a signal of forged or misrouted tokens, not as a reason to fetch a new key.

code.issue: A kid used in a path turns a header into traversal, and an attacker-chosen kid can name a key they hold. A fixed mapping limits selection to keys the verifier already trusts.

mcqs.question: What is the safe way to use the JWT kid header?
options: Look it up in a server-side map of trusted keys and reject unknown values
Use it to fetch the key from the URL it contains
Concatenate it into the key file path
Use it as the HMAC secret
mcqs.rationale: kid is attacker-controlled until the signature is verified, so it can only select from a set the server already trusts. Fetching URLs, path concatenation and using it as key material all hand control to the attacker.
